fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. The psalm says, "may the name of the God of Jacob protect you." Jacob is the man God renamed Israel (Genesis 32:28). The hope in that line is that this name keeps somebody safe in a hard day. I think that's a pretty good thing to have in your corner.
Yes, baker. The psalm says, "May He remember all your gifts and look favorably on your burnt offerings." Those two hopes ride together in the same verse. Then the verse ends with "Selah."

Close, but this one went the other way, friend. The psalm says, "May we shout for joy at your victory and raise a banner in the name of our God." Shouting and a banner are about as far from quiet as you can get. The hope in this line is for a victory celebrated out loud.

Right, baker. The hope here isn't a quiet day. The psalm says, "May we shout for joy at your victory and raise a banner in the name of our God." Shouting AND a banner. I'd be loud too, and I'd probably knock my hat off.

I get why you'd guess that, friend, since the song started with a day of trouble. But the turn goes the other way. The psalm says, "Now I know that the LORD saves His anointed…" That's a voice saying it knows, and fear isn't the word in this line.

I see the pull, friend. Chariots and horses sound like army gear. But the psalm says, "Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God." The contrast is between chariots and horses on one side and the name of the LORD on the other.

That's right, baker. The psalm ends, "O LORD, save the king." Then comes the line, "Answer us on the day we call." The psalm's own opening calls it a Psalm of David, so a king's name is already in the room.
Good thought, since burnt offerings show up earlier, friend. But the last line says, "O LORD, save the king." No priest is mentioned anywhere in this psalm. The one named in that cry is the king.
